verses.note: Japheth's descendants in chapter 10 include the coastland peoples to the north and west, among them Javan, the Greeks (10:2-5). Many Christian readers have seen a thematic fulfillment in the gospel reaching the Gentile world and bringing them into the blessings first given to Israel (Ephesians 2:13-19), though the verse itself makes no prediction of that kind.

Sheba and Seba, named here among the far peoples, reappear in Psalm 72:10 bringing gifts to Israel's king, and Isaiah 60:6 pictures those from Sheba bringing gold and frankincense to Zion. The peoples of the table become the peoples who will one day come to worship.

Shem's descendants include Elam, Assyria, the Arameans, and the Arabians as well as Eber. When God calls one man from this line, it will not be because the rest are outside his concern: the call is so that all the clans named here may be blessed (12:3).

The nations are named, counted, and placed before the story of Abram begins. The promise that all the families of the earth will be blessed (12:3) uses mishpechot, the same word as this verse; the table is the list of those the promise has in view.
The goal of Abram's calling is universal. The chosen family exists for the sake of the families of the whole earth, and Paul calls this promise the gospel announced in advance (Galatians 3:8).

Abram was called to be a blessing to the nations, and his first encounter with a foreign nation brings it plagues instead. The episode shows how the bearers of God's promise can obscure it, and how the outsider can be the one who speaks the truth.

From the start, the covenant household includes people of foreign birth. Belonging to Abraham's family was marked by the covenant sign, not by bloodline alone, which anticipates the Passover law for foreigners (Exodus 12:48) and the later inclusion of the nations.

The promise that the nations will be blessed through Abraham is the reason God reveals his judgment on Sodom. Abraham's calling concerns the nations, so he is brought into God's dealings with a Canaanite city, and his first response is to pray for it.

All the nations of the earth are in view at the climax of Abraham's story. Paul calls this promise the gospel announced in advance to Abraham (Galatians 3:8), and Peter applies it to the blessing that comes through Jesus (Acts 3:25-26).

Even at a moment of famine and fear, the promise to one family reaches past it to "all nations of the earth". God's dealings with Isaac are never only about Isaac's household; they are the channel of blessing for the world.

The promise to a single fugitive includes every family on earth. God's purpose for Jacob is never only about Jacob's safety, and Paul reads this promise as the gospel announced in advance to the Gentiles (Galatians 3:8).

Blessing flows outward from God's people to outsiders even when God's people are captives. The pattern returns in Jeremiah's instruction to the exiles to seek the welfare of the city where they have been carried (Jeremiah 29:7).

God promised Abraham that all the families of the earth would be blessed through his offspring (12:3, 28:14). Here, in a physical and partial way, the whole earth comes to one of Abraham's descendants for bread. The blessing reaches the nations before it reaches Joseph's own family.

Abraham's family was to be the channel of blessing to "all the families of the earth" (12:3). Here that promise touches the head of the world's greatest state, and the one blessing is a landless old herdsman who has come to him for food.

Egypt's elders escort the patriarch of Israel to his grave in the promised land. It is a small picture of the nations honoring the family of Abraham, though the same chariots will soon be turned against it.

The God who comes down to save sends a human messenger to carry out the rescue. Being ‘sent’ becomes the defining mark of a prophet, and Jesus uses the same pattern when he sends his disciples as the Father sent him (John 20:21).

The redeemed people leave Egypt already including outsiders. From its first day Israel was not a closed ethnic body, and the law that follows (verses 43 to 49) sets out how outsiders may join it fully.

The door into Israel's central rite is open to any foreigner willing to take the covenant sign, and once inside he is no longer second class. The Old Testament's openness to outsiders, seen in Rahab, Ruth, and Isaiah 56:6-7, has its legal root here.

The promise reaches beyond Israel's borders to every nation. The New Testament's commission to disciple all nations (Matthew 28:18-19) rests on the authority of the one who has received them from the Father.

One person's rescue becomes the occasion for the nations' conversion. The psalm moves from Israel to the ends of the earth, as the Abrahamic promise did, and the New Testament sees this movement carried out through the proclamation of the risen Christ.
The nations come bringing gifts to the king's court, a picture the Psalms and prophets widen into the ingathering of the nations to God's king (Psalm 72:10-11, Isaiah 60:5-6).

The nations come seeking the king of Israel, not by conquest but because he is lifted up as a sign. The verse is one of the Old Testament's clearest promises that the Messiah belongs to the Gentiles too. Jesus uses the image of being lifted up to draw all people to himself (John 12:32).

The return of God to Zion is a revelation to all humanity, not a private event for Israel. Luke extends his quotation to include this verse because it announces the salvation of God to all flesh, the theme of his two volumes.

What God does for Jerusalem is meant to be seen by the ends of the earth. The chapter moves from Zion to the nations and then, in verse 15, to the many nations and kings who will be silenced by the Servant.
The Servant's work reaches kings and nations who were never told of him. Paul made the second half of this verse his missionary principle: to preach where Christ had not been named (Romans 15:20-21).

The remnant scattered among many peoples is described as a blessing that comes from God and refreshes where it falls. Israel's dispersion is not only punishment; it places God's people among the nations as a means of his blessing, the promise to Abraham (Genesis 12:3) worked out in exile.

The oracle that began with judgment on the nations contains an inclusion of former enemies within God's people. The Philistines are not merely defeated; they are cleansed and counted among Judah's clans, a hope that the New Testament sees widening when the gospel reaches Gaza and Azotus, the Greek name for Ashdod (Acts 8:26-40).
The disciples' role in the world is given with their identity. Salt preserves and seasons only by contact, and a people that loses its distinctiveness loses its usefulness.

What Isaiah said of Israel and the Servant, Jesus says of his disciples. Their visible life is meant to bring glory to God, not to themselves, a purpose 6:1-18 guards against by forbidding religion performed to be seen.
Jesus' first act of public ministry is proclamation. The gospel is announced before it is explained, as news that calls for a response.
The call to follow includes the call to gather others. Discipleship and mission begin in the same sentence.
Jesus puts proclamation above popularity. The crowds want healing; he goes where the message has not yet been heard.

The first person in Mark sent to proclaim Jesus to Gentiles is a man who a few hours earlier lived among tombs. His commission is not to follow Jesus from place to place but to go home, and the verse gives that kind of witness its own dignity.

Mission begins with being called to Jesus and is carried out in his authority. The Twelve do not invent their message or their power; they extend his. Sending them in pairs builds companionship and witness into the work from the start.
The Twelve's mission is word and deed together: proclamation, exorcism, and healing. It is the pattern of Jesus' own ministry, handed on.

The first Gentile in Mark to ask Jesus for help is a woman, a foreigner, and the mother of a demonized child. The scene anticipates the church's mission to the nations and shows that the reach of Jesus' mercy is not decided by the categories the previous verses have just dismantled.

The saying states an order in God's saving plan, Israel first and then the nations, which Paul will restate in Romans 1:16 and follow in Acts 13:46. The word first also means that the Gentiles' turn is coming; the question is only when.
Only Mark keeps ‘for all the nations’. For his readers, many of them Gentiles, the verse showed that the God of Israel had always intended his house for them.

The gospel to all nations is a divine necessity, not an afterthought. Mark, written in all likelihood for a church that included Gentiles, puts the worldwide mission into the heart of Jesus' teaching about the future.

Jesus speaks of the gospel preached ‘in the whole world’ on the eve of his death, as he did in 13:10. The mission to the nations is not an afterthought to the cross but part of what he expects it to set in motion.
The first human confession of the Son of God in Mark comes from a Gentile, as the curtain is torn. The way the gospel will go to the nations (13:10) is already visible at the foot of the cross.

The risen Jesus sends the disciples who have just been rebuked. The commission does not wait for them to prove themselves; it is given to failed men and extends to the whole creation, which is the scope of the gospel from Mark's first line.
The mission is not left to the disciples alone. The one who sits at God's right hand works with them, and the message they carry is his word, confirmed by him.
Witness begins with people of low standing telling what they have seen and heard, the pattern of Acts 4:20. God's news does not wait for credentialed messengers.
Salvation is prepared ‘in the sight of all people’. From the child's first visit to the temple, Luke announces that the nations are included, the promise Acts carries out from Jerusalem to Rome.

Luke extends Isaiah's quotation to reach ‘all humanity’. From the start of Jesus' public story, the promise is universal, and Luke's two volumes end with Paul announcing that God's salvation has been sent to the Gentiles (Acts 28:28).

The mission belongs to the same necessity as the cross. The church does not decide to evangelize the nations as a strategy; the Scriptures and the risen Lord assign it, and it begins in the city that rejected him.
John uses the verb of sending (apostellō, pempō) for the Son about forty times, and in 20:21 Jesus sends the disciples as the Father sent him. The church's mission shares the purpose of this verse.
The verse is the pattern of Christian witness: the witness is glad to become smaller so that Christ is seen. John's success is measured by how many people leave him for Jesus.

The first witness in this chapter carries no credentials and makes no argument, only an invitation and an honest question. John treats her testimony as real witness (verse 39), the same word used for John the Baptist's testimony in chapter 1.

Jesus calls himself the one sent and his task a work to be completed. Mission in John begins with the Father sending the Son, and the disciples' sending (verse 38, 20:21) is drawn into that first sending.
The harvest is not only future. Jesus teaches the disciples to see people already turning to God where they expected nothing, and among a people they had learned to avoid.
No one owns the work. Those who sow and those who reap belong to one harvest and share its joy, which excludes both envy of predecessors and pride in results.

The sarcasm is an unconscious prophecy, like Caiaphas's word in 11:50-52. Jesus will be sought by Greeks (12:20-23), and after his going to the Father his message will reach the dispersion and the nations. John lets the scoffers name the church's mission before it begins.

The purpose of Paul's apostleship is the faith-obedience of every nation, for the sake of Christ's name. Mission in Romans is not recruitment to a group but the extension of Christ's rightful lordship over the peoples promised to Abraham (4:17-18).

The pairs of verse 14 cover every cultural and educational divide Paul's world recognized. The gospel is owed to all of them equally, and the apostle cannot choose his hearers by their sophistication.
Because God is one, the gospel must go to every nation on equal terms. Paul's mission to the Gentiles is here grounded not in strategy but in the Shema.
The goal of God's dealings with Pharaoh was that his name be proclaimed ‘in all the earth’. Even the hardening serves God's desire to be known among the nations, a theme Paul returns to in 11:11-15.

The God who named his own people ‘not my people’ in judgment can name outsiders ‘my people’ in mercy. Paul reads Hosea's promise as fulfilled in the Gentile mission, and Peter uses the same text of Gentile believers (1 Peter 2:10).
The one gospel has more than one field. God assigns different workers to different peoples, and the recognition of one another's callings is part of the church's unity.
The mission to the Gentiles is rooted in God's first promise to Abraham, not invented by the church. The Scripture that foresaw the nations' blessing sets the direction for the whole story.
The gospel's growth ‘in all the world’ echoes the creation blessing of fruitfulness. The spread of the message is presented as God's new creation filling the earth.
The mystery is Gentile inclusion in Christ. What Israel's prophets glimpsed (Isaiah 49:6) is now the content of the proclamation.
